# Get validated JSON results from models

Structured outputs is a capability on Amazon Bedrock that ensures model responses conform to user-defined JSON schemas and tool definitions, reducing the need for custom parsing and validation mechanisms in production AI deployments.

## Benefits

Structured outputs addresses critical challenges in production AI applications:

* Ensures schema compliance – Eliminates error rates and retry loops from prompt-based approaches
* Reduced development complexity – Removes the need for custom parsing and validation logic
* Lower operational costs – Reduces failed requests and retries
* Production reliability – Enables confident deployment of AI applications requiring predictable, machine-readable outputs

## How it works

Structured outputs constrains model responses to follow a specific schema, ensuring valid, parseable output for downstream processing. You can use structured outputs through two complementary mechanisms:

### JSON Schema output format

For InvokeModel API with Anthropic Claude models, use the

```
output_config.format
```

request field. With open weight models, use the

```
response_format
```

request field. For Converse APIs, use the

```
outputConfig.textFormat
```

request field. The model's response will conform to the specified JSON schema.

###### Note

The

```
output_format
```

field is deprecated. Use

```
output_config.format
```

instead.

### Strict tool use

Add the

```
strict: true
```

flag to tool definitions to enable schema validation on tool names and inputs. The model's tool calls will then follow the defined tool input schema.

These mechanisms can be used independently or together in the same request. Refer to Bedrock API documentation for more details.

### Request workflow

The following describes how Amazon Bedrock processes requests with structured outputs:

1. Initial request – You include either a JSON schema through the

   ```
   outputConfig.textFormat
   ```

   ,

   ```
   output_config.format
   ```

   , or

   ```
   response_format
   ```

   parameter or a tool definition with the

   ```
   strict: true
   ```

   flag in your inference request.
2. Schema validation – Amazon Bedrock validates the JSON schema format against the supported JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 subset. If the schema contains unsupported features, Amazon Bedrock returns a 400 error immediately.
3. First-time compilation – For new schemas, Amazon Bedrock compiles the grammar, which can take up to approximately 90 seconds.
4. Caching – Successfully compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from first access. Cached grammars are encrypted with AWS-managed keys.
5. Subsequent requests – Identical schemas from the same account use cached grammars, resulting in inference latency comparable to standard requests with minimal overhead.
6. Response – You receive standard inference responses with strict schema compliance.

## Supported JSON Schema features

The following JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 features are supported:

* All basic types:

  ```
  object
  ```

  ,

  ```
  array
  ```

  ,

  ```
  string
  ```

  ,

  ```
  integer
  ```

  ,

  ```
  number
  ```

  ,

  ```
  boolean
  ```

  ,

  ```
  null
  ```
* ```
  enum
  ```

  (strings, numbers, booleans, or nulls only)
* ```
  const
  ```

  ,

  ```
  anyOf
  ```

  ,

  ```
  allOf
  ```

  (with limitations)
* ```
  $ref
  ```

  ,

  ```
  $defs
  ```

  , and

  ```
  definitions
  ```

  (internal references only)
*

### Reference

# Modular JSON Schema combination

## Introduction

When writing computer programs of even moderate complexity, it's
commonly accepted that "structuring" the program into reusable
functions is better than duplicating code. Similarly, in JSON Schema, structuring your schema into reusable components is highly beneficial for anything beyond the most trivial cases.

Here, you will learn about the keywords used to combine JSON schemas modularly and see examples of their application.

## Schema Identification

Like any other code, schemas are easier to maintain if they can be
broken down into logical units that reference each other as necessary.
In order to reference a schema, we need a way to identify a schema.
Schema documents are identified by non-relative URIs.

Schema documents are not required to have an identifier, but you will
need one if you want to reference one schema from another. In this
documentation, we will refer to schemas with no identifier as
"anonymous schemas".

In the following sections we will see how the "identifier" for a
schema is determined.

URI terminology can sometimes be unintuitive. In this document, the
following definitions are used.

* **URI**
  [1] or
  **non-relative URI**: A full URI containing a scheme (`https`). It
  may contain a URI fragment (`#foo`). Sometimes this document will
  use "non-relative URI" to make it extra clear that relative URIs
  are not allowed.
* **relative reference**
  [2]:
  A partial URI that does not contain a scheme (`https`). It may
  contain a fragment (`#foo`).
* **URI-reference**
  [3]:
  A relative reference or non-relative URI. It may contain a URI
  fragment (`#foo`).
* **absolute URI**
  [4] A
  full URI containing a scheme (`https`) but not a URI fragment
  (`#foo`).

Even though schemas are identified by URIs, those identifiers are not
necessarily network-addressable. They are just identifiers. Generally,
implementations don't make HTTP requests (`https://`) or read from the
file system (`file://`) to fetch schemas. Instead, they provide a way to
load schemas into an internal schema database. When a schema is
referenced by it's URI identifier, the schema is retrieved from the
internal schema database.

## Base URI

Using non-relative URIs can be cumbersome, so any URIs used in JSON
Schema can be URI-references that resolve against the schema's base URI
resulting in a non-relative URI. This section describes how a schema's
base URI is determined.

Base URI determination and relative reference resolution is defined by
RFC-3986. If
you are familiar with how this works in HTML, this section should feel
very familiar.

### Retrieval URI

The URI used to fetch a schema is known as the "retrieval URI". It's
often possible to pass an anonymous schema to an implementation in which
case that schema would have no retrieval URI.

Let's assume a schema is referenced using the URI
`https://example.com/schemas/address` and the following schema is
retrieved.

schema

{ "type": "object", "properties": { "street\_address": { "type": "string" }, "city": { "type": "string" }, "state": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["street\_address", "city", "state"]}

The base URI for this schema is the same as the retrieval URI, `https://example.com/schemas/address`.

## $id

You can set the base URI by using the `$id` keyword at the root of the
schema. The value of `$id` is a URI-reference without a fragment that
resolves against the retrieval-uri. The resulting URI is
the base

Hyderabad is rationing piped water to once every three days and fining pubs up to Rs 20,000 for washing floors with drinking water. But videos of water gushing onto streets in two localities have left residents asking who will answer for those leaks.  
  
In one video, from Maula Ali, Manjeera water is seen running down a road. In the other, from SR Nagar, water spills from a pump outside JJ Hospital.  
  
Both clips spread on social media, with users asking who was responsible for letting water go to waste in the middle of a crisis.  
  
“Restaurants and pubs were asked to pay a Rs 20,000 fine for wasting water. Who should be penalised for this pump, which is leaking water?” asked Mohammed Ilyas, who posted the SR Nagar video on Instagram.  
  
Fines for some:  
The Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply and Sewerage Board (HMWSSB) has been fining people, restaurants and pubs between Rs 5,000 and Rs 20,000 for wasting water while cleaning their premises. One city pub was recently fined Rs 20,000.  
  
From November 1, water tankers caught spilling drinking water on the way will also be fined Rs 5,000. HMWSSB Managing Director K Ashok Reddy issued the order on October 24 after the board found tankers being overfilled and water splashing onto roads.  
  
Tankers with leaks, missing lids or loose covers will not be filled until they are repaired.  
  
The Maula Ali leak has struck a nerve because the Manjeera is one of the sources under the most strain. The board expects a shortfall of about 100 million gallons a day (MGD) from Singur and Manjeera between January and August.

# HMWSSB warns residents against water wastage, threatens to disconnect services

Published - September 21, 2026 07:45 pm IST - HYDERABAD

The Hindu Bureau

SEE ALL
Remove

The Hyderabad Metropolitan Water Supply & Sewerage Board (HMWS&SB) has issued serious warning against water wastage, after imposing penalties in five such instances on Monday. Second time offenders will attract disconnection of water supply, it warned.

All the five penalised were residents of Jubilee Hills, and found to have been wasting water, during inspections conducted by the Board officials.

The inspections will be intensified in the coming days, and second time offenders will be penalised through disconnection of water supply, the note warned.

Using drinking water to wash floor and vehicles, leaving the tap open, and not shutting down the pump set even after overhead tank overflows are some of the instances of water wastage, as shared by the Board.

Despite awareness campaigns and warnings, the users are still found resorting to the same practices, calling for penalties. The penalties which had started with just ₹1000 per instance, have over the time risen to ₹5,000, then ₹10,000 and now ₹20,000. Still the violations continue to persist. the note said.

Leakages in the water supply network too will be plugged by officials within 24 hours of identification, and in case of dereliction of duties, action will be taken against officials and staff too. The water board’s drinking water pipeline extends to 15,000 kilometres in the city, to plug leakages in which, a special action plan is being be taken up. The officials have been directed to identify locations with frequent leakages and provide permanent solutions.
